title: The challenge: Minimizing thermal resistance
text:
The challenge: Minimizing thermal resistance
At flow rates corresponding to Reynolds numbers below 2,300, the flow is laminar which creates significant thermal resistance in the fluid
In the region with more developed turbulence  (2800+ Reynolds) the resistance in the fluid is minimal
In most systems today, the brine fluid flow rate varies across the season. This means a significant part of the running hours is in the laminar state (<2,300 Reynolds)
High flow rates generate high pressuredrop

title: Heat transfer (Nusselt) correlations
text:
## Heat transfer (Nusselt number) correlations

Regime-split correlation for the finned collector, blended with the smooth-pipe
laminar Nusselt number `Nu_smooth,lam`:

- **Laminar / low-Re region (0 ≤ Re ≤ 1700):**

  `Nu_lam^reg = sqrt( Nu_smooth,lam^2 + [ (5.5 × 10^-7) · Re^1.77 · Pr^0.5 ]^2 )`

- **Transition / unsteady region (1700 < Re ≲ 3300):**

  `Nu_turb^reg = sqrt( Nu_smooth,lam^2 + [ 0.86 · (Re − 1699)^0.39 · Pr^0.32 ]^2 )`

The accompanying Nu-vs-Re plot compares the fitted "Nu alternating fins corr"
curve against the Gnielinski correlation (`Nu_Gni`) and the DNS data points
("Nu alternating fins DNS"). The finned correlation shows a sharp rise in Nu
beginning around Re ≈ 1700, well below the smooth-pipe turbulent transition
(~Re 2300).

source: Correlations for pressure drop and heat transfer.pptx
title: Pressure drop (friction factor) correlation
text:
## Pressure drop (friction factor) correlation

A blending weight `w` smoothly transitions the friction factor between the
laminar and turbulent expressions across the 1700–2300 window:

- **Blending weight:**

  `w = ( 1 + exp[ −5 · ( (Re − 1700) / (2300 − 1700) − 0.5 ) ] )^(−1)`

- **Combined friction factor:**

  `f_comb^reg = (1 − w) · (64 / Re) + w · [ −1.8 · log10( 6.9 / Re ) ]^(−2)`

Here `64/Re` is the laminar (Hagen–Poiseuille) friction factor and the
`[−1.8·log10(6.9/Re)]^(−2)` term is a Haaland-type turbulent friction factor.
The friction-factor-vs-Re plot compares `f_analytical_smooth`,
`f_Haaland_smooth`, and the fitted `f_corr_alt` curve against the DNS points for
the alternating-fin geometry.

title: TurboCollector headline performance figures
text: The TurboCollector (MuoviTech, patented) maintains turbulent/unsteady flow at up to 22% lower flow rates than a smooth pipe. This gives up to 80% reduced fluid (convective) thermal resistance, up to 3.6 degrees C higher brine temperature, and up to 11% COP (coefficient of performance) improvement of the heat pump. In the 1,700-2,300 Reynolds window the convective heat transfer increases by up to 300-600%, with only a few percent (negligible) pressure-drop penalty outside that window. Product life expectancy is 50+ years; SKZ approved.

title: Why flow regime matters (the problem)
text: Borehole thermal resistance is R_tot = R_w + R_p + R_f (water/grout, pipe wall, brine convective). The brine convective resistance R_f can be ~50% of the total at certain conditions. Below ~2,300 Reynolds flow is laminar with poor mixing and low heat transfer; unsteady flow gives 5-10x higher heat transfer. Real systems run at 1,300<Re<3,300 over the season, spending much of the year in the laminar region where smooth pipes perform worst. The TurboCollector's alternating helical fins trigger unsteady flow down to Re<1,800.

title: The Chalmers DNS study (summary)
text: Study 'Evaluation of internal fin designs for ground collectors' by Niklas Hidman, Eskil Nilsson, Kim Johansson, Daniel Almgren (Chalmers University of Technology). Used fully-resolved 3D Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS). Evaluated 30+ fin designs. Best design: alternating helical fins, 0.6 mm height, 16 fins, twisting 360 degrees over 0.7 m. Result vs smooth pipe: +300-600% convective heat transfer in the 1,700-2,300 Reynolds region, only a few percent higher pressure drop outside it.

title: Geothermal energy basic training part 1 @ 00:01:24
text: There is also something called energy piles which is seems to be similar to the borehole heat exchangers or the borehole storage, but in this case it's the foundation of the building. The foundation piles of a building that are used to collect heating or cooling from the ground. Those piles are typically between 6 and 20 metres deep, made of concrete or steel. So it's a different type and it will never cover the entire heating or cooling load of a building, but it is a possibility to make use of the building foundation. The ones that I've mentioned now, they use heat from the sun. It's the sun that provides heat to the ground and the ground absorbs this heat and that is the the heat source, the main heat source. There is also a component from the the centre of the ground, but that is rather small for this kind of application, so it's mostly solar heat. It could also be waste heat or waste cooling from buildings that are stored in the ground.

title: Geothermal energy basic training part 1 @ 00:02:40
text: Then there are the more infrastructural types of geothermal energy, which is pit and cavern storage. PTES and CTES typically used in conjunction with thermal networks. So it's actively stored heating and cooling. It could be excess heat from from industrial processes from waste heat. It could also be it could be district heating that is produced with from some kind of source heating source. They are typically large scale and nothing that you use just for one single building. Then there is the exception at the special case which is the deep pure thermal systems where the component from the sun is very small. They have very deep boreholes, typically more than a kilometre deep, maybe several kilometres, and extract heat from either aquifers, deep aquifers down in at several kilometres depth, or they make use of fractures in the ground and extract vapour, heat, hot vapour from the rock and that can be used. That's mostly heat from the core of the Earth could be at high temperature and is could be used for heating or for power production if the temperature is high enough.

PTES and CTES typically used in conjunction with thermal networks. So it's actively stored heating and cooling. It could be excess heat from from industrial processes from waste heat. It could also be it could be district heating that is produced with from some kind of source heating source. They are typically large scale and and nothing that you use just for one single building. text:
So first the recap of what pressure drop is and how it affects the system. So the pressure drop in flow system like our collectors is an energy loss that is created due to friction and resistance within the pipe and the components like valves and other things in the geothermal system. And this affects the flow because the flow is driven by pressure. We need to have different pressures within the system to get the the fluid moving And the pump. The circulation pump that we have in the system is the pump is creating the pressure and this pressure is sort of eaten up or used up by the pressure drop within the pipes due to friction. And the pump done needs to overcome this. It needs to add more power to to handle this pressure drop. And if it can't add more power, then the result will be that the flow rate will be lower. So the flow of the fluid will be slower and slower. And this is something that we could see in these graphs of the circulation pump.

That means that the pressure drop will be lower in this part than in the longer part and therefore more fluid where the flow rate will increase in the short borehole and decrease in the longer borehole. And this is creating unwanted situation because that means that we are shifting the energy outtake. It will no longer be equal between the boreholes and in fact we will take more heat from the short borehole than we do from the long borehole. And this is something that we would like to avoid. And therefore we in our manifolds we are installing balancing valves. And if we were to install a balancing valve in this short borehole, we would need to close the valve more and more and more until we have added enough pressure drop so that it will be equal to the pressure drop that it would be for the missing pipe in this section.

title: TC_final test time (narration) @ 00:00:00
text: In a well designed geothermal system, at maximum load the fluid flow rate is high enough for creating fully turbulent flow. Turbulence creates good mixing of the fluid which reduces the thermal resistance of the system, increasing the fluid temperature and increasing the performance of the heat pump. However, during a large part of the year, the system are not running at maximum flow rates due to lower heating requirements. With a smooth probe, the flow becomes laminar with poor mixing. This is bad for the heat transfer and gives a lower fluid temperature and a lower efficiency of the heat pump. When instead using MuoviTech patented TurboCollector, the flow rates continue to be turbulent at reduced flow rates, maintaining high heat transfer, increased fluid temperature, and improved efficiency of the heat pump. Independent research has shown that MuoviTech's unique and patented fin design with alternating fin directions is creating the most optimal heat transfer. The study concludes that MuoviTech's TurboCollector creates up to 600% increase in heat transfer.

source: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] [webinar]
title: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] @ 01:08:00
text: Yes, exactly. Increasingly there are even larger installations now, with several dozen kilometres of collector. The exchangers are also getting deeper. A dozen-plus years ago the standard was 100 m borehole heat exchangers, but now drilling companies in Poland are specialising more, gaining experience, and go down even to 300 m. This gives better geothermal temperatures and better efficiency. And that is exactly why we are talking today about how to recover that heat better, because you have to pay attention to this installation. We are talking about kilometres of piping underground. You mentioned geothermal energy, let's clarify that. About 80% of the geothermal energy we exploit comes from the Earth's crust, from thermonuclear processes inside our planet. About 20% is residual heat from the planet's formation billions of years ago, from bombardment by celestial bodies and volcanic activity. Additionally there are trace amounts from solar radiation, a very small fraction of geothermal energy. Of course in shallow ground sources some solar energy is present. For example horizontal exchangers, less popular today, are buried shallow and get more sun. We divide exchangers into vertical (boreholes) and horizontal ones (spiral, linear), which take energy from precipitation, cosmic radiation and the sun.

source: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] [webinar]
title: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] @ 01:10:00
text: But let's return to the multi-kilometre vertical system. Since we have invested in kilometres of pipes with fluids, how do we recover the heat better? Michal, please. Exactly. The whole borehole heat exchanger is one big system: the energy carrier (an antifreeze fluid), the vertical exchanger (our vertical probe/pipes), the filling material, and the ground itself. Imagine a 300 m exchanger profile drilled through the planet's layers, with different temperatures at different depths. The whole system depends on correctly executing this vertical heat exchanger. The two most important parameters characterising borehole heat exchangers are the borehole thermal resistance and lambda, the thermal conductivity. We practically cannot change lambda or the ground's thermal conductivity, because we cannot change the earth's rock and lithological layers. We have what we have. But we can improve the thermal resistance, because there can be different filling materials, in the form of highly heat-conductive thermal cements (grout). We can also apply different flow regimes in the vertical exchanger, laminar or turbulent, and use different pipe constructions installed by drillers and installers as the vertical heat exchanger.

source: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] [webinar]
title: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] @ 01:12:01
text: So what is your idea to limit these losses, or to increase heat recovery? As I mentioned, we cannot influence the cylinder, the Earth's crust, but we have huge influence on the flows, the hydraulic resistances, on what happens inside between the vertical pipe exchanger and the energy carrier. Because there can be two flow types, laminar and turbulent. Look at the slide on screen: with turbulent flow we can significantly reduce the borehole heat-exchanger thermal resistance, but this generates additional hydraulic losses. Such turbulent flow generates extra hydraulic resistance, so we would have to select bigger circulation pumps for the designed flow, which generates higher energy bills to drive those circulation pumps. But we have a great product to overcome the difficulties caused by turbulent flow: the TurboCollector probe, shown on screen. The TurboCollector probe is equipped with internal fins (lamellae) that significantly improve the flow inside the pipe. It is specially designed, with a specially calculated number of fins, of the right thickness, with a specially designed rotation. That is, the internal spin swirls, with rotation in one direction and then the other.

source: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] [webinar]
title: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] @ 01:14:05
text: It is a bit like a barrel, a rifled gun barrel. Exactly, and you are not the only one who thinks so; many people handling our product for the first time say it looks like a rifled barrel or a cannon. But the fins have a special task: to make the energy-carrier fluid flow turbulently and significantly reduce the thermal resistance of the heat exchanger, improving its efficiency. On our website there is a full report done by a Swedish university (Chalmers), where, based on our patented TurboCollector, a comparative study was made with other fin variants, with different swirl variations and spin designs. As mentioned, we have a special rotation that goes forward and backward, but rotation can also occur in one direction only. The study unambiguously confirmed that this back-and-forth rotation has the biggest effect on the borehole heat-exchanger thermal resistance, and thus on the heat exchange between the ground and the energy carrier. By lowering the exchanger's thermal resistance we can deliver much better glycol / carrier temperatures to the heat pump's evaporator, and thus significantly raise the heat pump's COP.

source: Forum Branzowe (Globenergia) - MuoviTech TurboCollector interview with Michal Szczytowski [translated from Polish] [webinar]

text: That is the efficiency. Yes, the efficiency, so we lower electricity bills, because honestly the temperatures from the lower heat source have the biggest impact on the heat pump's COP. You compared turbulent flow to classic laminar flow. To put it in simple terms: when we disturb the fluid flow in the probe we insert deep into the ground, more molecules of the fluid contact the probe wall and heat is picked up from the ground better. Exactly. Imagine that with an ordered, laminar flow we heat the carrier fastest right at the exchanger walls, while in the middle the faster-moving fluid stays much colder and there is no mixing, so the temperature is much worse.
